questions.q: In the H-then-S circuit, why does checking that H is unitary (H†H=I) matter before trusting the circuit's output?
options: Unitary matrices are the only matrices capable of being written down as code
Checking unitarity has no real mathematical consequence for the circuit's behavior
Non-unitary matrices always produce negative probabilities, which is impossible to compute
A unitary matrix is guaranteed to preserve normalization, so applying it to a valid normalized state produces another valid normalized state with probabilities summing to 1
questions.explain: Unitarity is specifically what guarantees that a valid (normalized) input state produces a valid (normalized) output state -- without it, there's no guarantee the resulting amplitudes would even correspond to real probabilities.

questions.q: After applying both H and S to |0⟩, the final probabilities are [0.5, 0.5] -- identical to what H alone would have produced. Why doesn't applying S change the probabilities?
options: S gates never have any mathematical effect on a quantum state whatsoever
The probabilities only appear unchanged due to a rounding error in the calculation
S multiplies the second amplitude by a phase factor (i), which changes its angle on the complex plane but not its magnitude, and measurement probability depends only on magnitude
S secretly undoes everything that H did to the state
questions.explain: This is the phase-vs-magnitude distinction from the complex-exponentials lesson: S rotates the second amplitude's phase (multiplying by i = e^(i*pi/2)) without changing |amplitude|^2, so the measured probabilities stay the same.

questions.q: The lesson notes that a phase gate's effect 'becomes visible the moment a later gate, like another Hadamard, interferes it against something else.' What does this reveal about phase in quantum computing?
options: A phase that's invisible to a direct measurement can still be mathematically real and physically meaningful, becoming observable once it interferes with another amplitude via a subsequent gate
Phase has no real physical meaning and can always be safely ignored
Once a phase is applied, it can never again affect the outcome of any future computation
Phase only matters if a measurement is taken in a completely different basis
questions.explain: This is precisely why real quantum algorithms use phase: even though a single measurement right after a phase gate can't detect it, later interference (e.g., another Hadamard) converts that hidden phase information into a measurable probability difference.

questions.q: Per the lesson's checklist, what must happen before applying any gate in a multi-qubit circuit?
options: Every qubit must first be measured individually
The full multi-qubit state space must be built via tensor products before any gate is applied
All gates in the circuit must be identical to each other
The circuit must be converted into a classical bit string first
questions.explain: Chapter 6's tensor-product material is exactly what constructs the combined state space for multiple qubits -- this has to happen before gates can be correctly applied to the joint system.

questions.q: What is the overall point of this capstone lesson, connecting back to the whole course?
options: Every mathematical tool taught across the course (vectors, matrices, complex numbers, unitarity, tensor products, probability, phase) is not abstract for its own sake -- it is exactly the toolkit needed to trace through one real, small quantum circuit
The capstone is unrelated to any of the course's earlier chapters
The capstone proves that quantum circuits cannot actually be analyzed using ordinary mathematics
The capstone introduces entirely new mathematical concepts never covered earlier in the course
questions.explain: The capstone deliberately ties every step of a real circuit trace back to a specific earlier chapter, showing the course's math isn't abstract exercise -- it's the literal toolkit used to understand real quantum circuit behavior.
